title: Local linear convergence of gradient methods for overparameterized Gaussian mixtures
claim: A standard slow-converging baseline stalls, while interleaving occasional special long steps yields repeated sharp drops and much faster local convergence.
layout: 2 side-by-side log-scale line plots, shared legend style, markers at step drops
description: Two side-by-side line plots with a log-scale y-axis and iteration (0 to 200) on the x-axis. The left panel is titled "Loss" and shows KL divergence. The right panel is titled "Parameter distance" and shows a weighted sum of squared distances between student and teacher means. Each panel has a dashed blue curve for Gradient EM and a solid green curve for GDPolyak. The blue curve decays slowly and smoothly across all 200 iterations. The green curve follows the blue curve at first. After that it moves in a staircase pattern, with gentle slopes interrupted by sharp vertical drops. Hollow square markers sit at the bottom of each drop. The green curve ends near iteration 105 about two orders of magnitude below the blue curve. Both panels have a legend at the upper right and light grey gridlines. The eye goes first to the green staircase.
caption: Local acceleration for loss and parameter distance. The square markers indicate iterates obtained with Polyak steps, which are interleaved with several steps of gradient descent. In this instance, we have dimension $d = 5$, $m = 3$ teacher components, and $n = 20$ student components.
abstract: We study the problem of learning Gaussian mixture models under overparameterization. Prior work has shown that while overparameterization is essential for avoiding spurious local optima and enables global recovery of the ground-truth model using the gradient-EM (expectation-maximization) algorithm, it can dramatically slow down the local rate of convergence. Under certain assumptions on the mixture weights, we show that a standard divergence measure minimized by statistical learning procedures possesses a manifold of slow growth on which the well-known Polyak stepsize reduces the loss geometrically, and design a gradient-based method that converges to minimizers at a locally linear rate. Additionally, we show that our method converges to nearly optimal solutions -- up to a natural misspecification threshold -- for mixtures with arbitrary weights. At a high level, the method alternates between several "short" gradient descent steps that approach the manifold and "long" Polyak steps that contract the distance to minimizers. Our results suggest that slow convergence is not an intrinsic challenge of overparameterization, but can be overcome by exploiting the favorable structure of the loss landscape.
